title: Undoing the last commit
text: git reset --soft HEAD~1 rewinds the most recent commit while keeping your staged changes intact. git reset --hard throws the changes away entirely, so use it only when you truly want to discard work.

title: Detached HEAD state
text: A detached HEAD happens when you check out a commit hash directly instead of a branch. New commits made in this state belong to no branch, can vanish after the next checkout, and are hard to recover unless you create a branch to hold them.

title: Safer force pushes
text: git push --force-with-lease refuses to overwrite the remote branch if someone else pushed in the meantime. It is the safer alternative to a plain --force when you rewrite history on a shared branch.

title: Removing untracked files
text: git clean -fd deletes untracked files and directories from the working tree. Run it with -n first for a dry run that shows what would be removed before anything is actually erased.

title: Stashing work in progress
text: git stash shelves uncommitted changes so the working tree is clean again. git stash pop later restores the shelved snapshot onto whatever branch is checked out.

title: Rebase versus merge
text: Rebasing replays your commits on top of another branch and produces a linear history. Merging preserves the true order of events but adds a merge commit that some teams find noisy.

title: Finding a bad commit with bisect
text: git bisect runs a binary search over history to locate the commit that introduced a bug. You mark each checkout as good or bad and git halves the remaining range until the culprit is found.

title: Cherry-picking a commit
text: git cherry-pick copies a single commit from another branch onto the current one. It creates a new commit with the same changes but a different hash, which matters when the branches later merge.

title: What the reflog records
text: The reflog records every position HEAD has pointed to, even across resets and rebases. A commit no branch references is still reachable from the reflog, so you can check out its hash and create a branch to hold it.

title: Ignoring an already tracked file
text: Adding a path to .gitignore does not stop tracking a file that was already committed. Run git rm --cached on it to drop it from the index while keeping the copy on disk.

title: Shallow clones for CI
text: A shallow clone with --depth 1 downloads only the latest snapshot instead of the full history. Cloning a huge repository this way is dramatically faster, which is why CI pipelines use it.

title: Working with submodules
text: A submodule pins an external repository at an exact commit inside your project. After cloning the parent, submodules must be initialized and updated separately or their directories stay empty.

title: Finding files by name
text: find . -name '*.log' walks a directory tree and prints every path matching the pattern. Combine it with -delete or -exec to act on each result, such as removing old log files in bulk to free space.

title: Searching file contents with grep
text: grep -r searches recursively through folders for lines matching a pattern. Add -i to ignore case and -n to show line numbers alongside each match.

title: Stopping processes with signals
text: kill sends a signal to a process by pid; the default SIGTERM lets the target shut down cleanly. SIGKILL, sent with kill -9, cannot be caught or ignored and ends the process immediately.

title: Which process owns a port
text: lsof -i :8080 lists the process listening on a port, which is the fastest way to find what is already bound there. ss and netstat give a wider view of every open socket on the machine.

title: Diagnosing full disks
text: du -sh reports the total size of a directory tree, while df -h shows free capacity per filesystem. When a machine runs low on disk space, large build caches and old logs are the usual suspects.

title: File permissions with chmod
text: chmod changes permissions using octal digits for owner, group and others. 755 grants the owner full access and everyone else read and execute, the usual setting for scripts and directories.

title: Watching logs with tail
text: tail -f streams new lines as they are appended, the quickest way to watch a log in real time. tail -n 100 prints the last hundred lines first so you have context before following.

title: Pipes and redirection
text: The pipe operator sends the stdout of one command into the stdin of the next. Redirect output into a file with >, append with >>, and capture stderr separately with 2>.

title: Scheduling jobs with cron
text: cron runs scheduled jobs at fixed times defined in a crontab. Each entry has five time fields followed by the command, so a task can fire every minute, nightly, or once a week.

title: SSH key authentication
text: ssh-keygen creates a public and private key pair for logging in without typing a password. ssh-copy-id installs the public key into the server's authorized_keys file to enable it.

title: Environment variables
text: export makes a shell variable visible to child processes as an environment variable. printenv shows everything currently set, which helps when a program cannot see the configuration you expected.

title: Fanning out work with xargs
text: xargs turns lines from stdin into arguments for another command. Paired with find, it runs one operation across many files at once instead of invoking the command per file.

title: 404 versus 410
text: A 404 Not Found says the resource is missing without promising anything about the future. A 410 Gone states it existed and was deliberately removed, a hint that clients should delete their references.

title: 500, 502 and 503 errors
text: A 500 means the server itself crashed while handling the request. A 502 Bad Gateway means an upstream server returned garbage to a proxy, and a 503 means the service is temporarily unavailable or overloaded.

title: 401 versus 403
text: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid credentials and the client should authenticate. 403 Forbidden means the identity is known but access to the resource is denied anyway.

title: CORS and cross-origin requests
text: Browsers enforce the same-origin rule: a page may only issue fetch or API requests to its own origin unless the target server opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. The preflight OPTIONS request asks whether the real cross-origin call is permitted.

title: Connection refused errors
text: ECONNREFUSED means the target machine actively rejected the connection because nothing is listening on that port. Check that the service is running and bound to the address and port you are dialing.

title: Timeouts and retries
text: Every network call needs a deadline so a request does not sit waiting forever on a connection that will never produce a reply. Retries belong on top, with exponential backoff and jitter so a struggling service is not stampeded.

title: Idempotent methods and retry safety
text: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating them yields the same result. POST is not, which is why payment APIs accept an idempotency key that makes a retried request safe to process twice.

title: HTTP caching headers
text: Cache-Control and ETag headers let clients reuse a stored response instead of fetching it again from the origin server. A conditional request with If-None-Match returns 304 Not Modified when nothing changed.

title: TLS and the HTTPS handshake
text: HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS, which negotiates encryption keys during a handshake before any data flows. The certificate proves the server's identity and is validated against trusted authorities.

title: DNS resolution and TTL
text: DNS translates a domain name into an IP address before a connection can open. Results are cached for the record's TTL, which is why an old address lingers for a while after you change where a name points.

title: WebSockets for live updates
text: A WebSocket upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent two-way channel. It suits chat and live dashboards where the server pushes updates the moment they happen instead of the client polling.

title: Rate limiting and 429
text: A 429 Too Many Requests response tells the client it exceeded a rate limit. The Retry-After header says how long to back off before sending traffic again.

title: Virtual environments
text: A virtual environment gives each project an isolated set of installed packages so versions never clash across projects. Create one with python -m venv and activate it before running pip install.

title: Mutable default arguments
text: Default argument values are evaluated once when the function is defined, so a mutable default like a list is the same object on every call. Use None as the default and build a fresh list inside the function.

title: The GIL and true parallelism
text: The global interpreter lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help for IO-bound work, but CPU-bound code needs multiprocessing to use every core.

title: Handling exceptions
text: Wrap risky operations in try and except blocks to handle errors like FileNotFoundError instead of crashing. Catch specific exception types; a bare except hides real bugs and swallows keyboard interrupts.

title: Generators for streaming data
text: A generator yields items one at a time instead of building the whole list up front. That is how you stream a very large file without holding it all in memory.

title: List comprehensions
text: A list comprehension builds a list from an iterable in one readable expression, replacing a loop with append. Keep them to a single condition or two; past that a plain loop reads better.

title: Dataclasses
text: The dataclass decorator generates __init__, __repr__ and equality methods from class attributes. It removes the boilerplate of hand-writing constructors for classes that mostly hold data.

title: Concurrency with asyncio
text: asyncio multiplexes many network operations on a single thread with an event loop. An async def function suspends at each await, so other coroutines run while one waits on the network.

title: Type hints and mypy
text: Type hints annotate arguments and return values so tools can check correctness before the code runs. mypy reads them and flags mismatched types, catching a class of bugs without any tests.

title: pytest fixtures and parametrize
text: A pytest fixture provides reusable setup and teardown to any test that names it as an argument. Parametrize runs one test body against many input cases, each reported separately.

title: Serialization: json versus pickle
text: json serializes plain data structures to a portable text format any language can read. pickle handles arbitrary Python objects but is unsafe to load from untrusted sources, since it can execute code.

title: Debugging with pdb
text: pdb is the built-in interactive debugger; calling breakpoint() drops you into it at that line. You can step through code, inspect variables and evaluate expressions at the prompt.

title: Inner join versus left join
text: An inner join returns only rows with a match in both tables. A left join keeps every row from the left table and fills the missing side with NULL when there is no match.

title: Indexes and query speed
text: An index is a sorted structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. A query filtering on an unindexed column degrades as the table grows, until an index brings it back to milliseconds.

title: The N+1 query problem
text: The N+1 problem happens when code fires one query per item in a loop instead of a single batched query. Fetching everything with a join or an IN clause removes the extra round trips.

title: Transactions and atomicity
text: A transaction groups statements so they either all commit or all roll back together. That guarantee keeps a money transfer consistent even if the server dies halfway through the updates.

title: SQL injection
text: SQL injection lets an attacker smuggle commands through user input concatenated into a query string. Parameterized queries with placeholders keep input as data, never executable code.

title: GROUP BY and HAVING
text: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing a value so aggregates like COUNT and SUM apply per group. HAVING filters on those aggregates after grouping, which WHERE cannot do.

title: Reading query plans
text: EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer chose, including whether it scans the whole table or walks an index. Reading the plan is the first step in figuring out why a query is slow.

title: Schema migrations
text: A migration is a versioned script that alters the schema so every environment applies the same change in the same order. Each one should have a rollback path in case the deploy goes wrong.

title: Normalization tradeoffs
text: Normalization removes duplicated facts so an update touches one row instead of many. Denormalizing reintroduces copies deliberately to make hot read paths cheaper, trading write complexity for read speed.

title: Connection pooling
text: Opening a database connection is expensive, so a pool keeps a set of them ready to reuse. Without pooling, a busy web service churns through connections and exhausts the database.

title: Images versus containers
text: An image is an immutable template; a container is a running instance of it. Many containers can start from the same image, each with its own writable state.

title: Layer caching in builds
text: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer that is cached and reused when nothing above it changed. Order matters: put steps that rarely change, like dependency installs, before frequently edited source files.

title: Persisting data with volumes
text: Files written inside a container disappear when the container is removed. A volume mounts storage that lives on the host, so the data survives restarts and remains after the container is recreated.

title: Publishing container ports
text: docker run -p 8080:80 publishes container port 80 on host port 8080. Without a published port, a service inside the container is unreachable from outside the host.

title: Multi-service apps with compose
text: docker compose defines a multi-service application in one YAML file. A single command starts the app together with its database and cache, wired onto a shared network.

title: Memory limits and OOMKilled
text: A container that exceeds its memory limit is killed by the kernel and shows an OOMKilled status. Raise the limit or fix the leak, and keep the configured limit close to real usage.

title: Multi-stage builds
text: A multi-stage build compiles the app in one stage and copies only the finished binary into a slim final stage. The production image stays small and ships no compilers or build tools.

title: Slim base images
text: Choosing a minimal base like alpine or distroless cuts an image from gigabytes to tens of megabytes. Less inside the image also means fewer packages an attacker can exploit.

title: Healthchecks and restart policies
text: A healthcheck probes the container periodically so the runtime knows whether the app inside is actually serving or has stopped responding. Combined with a restart policy, a crashed or unhealthy container is brought back automatically.

title: Registries and image tags
text: docker push uploads an image to a registry under a name and tag, and docker pull fetches it elsewhere. Tags are mutable pointers, so pin a digest when you need the exact same image every time.

title: Storing passwords safely
text: Passwords must be stored as slow salted hashes using bcrypt or argon2, never encrypted or in plain text. The salt makes identical passwords hash differently, defeating precomputed lookup tables.

title: JWTs and stateless auth
text: A JWT carries signed claims about the user, so a service can trust the token itself instead of asking a central store on every request. The signature stops tampering, but the payload is only base64 encoded, not secret.

title: Cross-site scripting
text: XSS happens when text from outside ends up rendered as markup, and any script it contains executes with the page's privileges in the victim's browser. Escape on output by default and set a Content-Security-Policy as a second layer.

title: Cross-site request forgery
text: CSRF tricks a logged-in visitor's browser into submitting a request they never intended, riding on their cookies. Anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies stop the forged request from being accepted.

title: Leaked secrets and rotation
text: An API key committed to a repository must be treated as leaked and rotated immediately, because history keeps a copy even after the file is deleted. Keep secrets in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in source control.

title: OAuth authorization flow
text: OAuth lets a user grant an app limited access to their account on another service without sharing their password. The app receives a scoped access token it can use until the grant expires or is revoked.

title: Least privilege
text: Every credential and role should carry the minimum access needed for its job. When a token leaks, narrow scopes turn a catastrophe into a contained incident.

title: Certificate expiry
text: TLS certificates expire, and an expired one takes the whole site down with browser warnings users cannot bypass. Automate renewal and alert well before the deadline instead of relying on memory.

title: Vulnerable dependencies
text: Most application vulnerabilities arrive through outdated third-party packages, not your own code. Automated scanners audit the lockfile and open upgrade pull requests when a known issue is published.

title: Two-factor authentication
text: A second factor means a stolen password alone is not enough to get in. Time-based one-time codes or hardware keys block the vast majority of account takeover attempts.

title: The event loop
text: JavaScript runs on a single thread with an event loop that processes queued callbacks. Long synchronous work blocks the loop, and the page cannot respond to clicks or render updates until it finishes.

title: Promises and async/await
text: A promise represents a value that arrives later, and await suspends the current function until it settles. Errors propagate through rejected promises, so a missing catch means a silent failure.

title: Closures
text: A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has returned. It is how callbacks keep access to surrounding state.

title: Loose versus strict equality
text: The == operator coerces types before comparing, producing surprises like empty string equaling zero. Strict === compares without coercion and is the sane default.

title: Lockfiles and reproducible installs
text: The lockfile pins the exact version of every package in the dependency tree. Committing it means every machine and CI run installs identical versions instead of whatever is newest that day.

title: Debounce and throttle
text: Debouncing delays a handler until events stop arriving; throttling caps how often it fires. Both keep a scroll or keystroke listener from firing hundreds of times per second.

title: Listener leaks
text: An event listener that is added but never removed keeps its closure and DOM nodes alive forever. In a long-lived page these forgotten listeners pile up into a memory leak that slowly grows, eating memory the page never gives back.

title: Tree shaking and bundle size
text: Tree shaking drops exports nothing imports, shrinking the bundle the browser must download. It only works when modules avoid side effects the bundler cannot see through.

title: Greedy versus lazy quantifiers
text: Quantifiers are greedy by default, matching as much text as possible before backtracking. Adding ? after one makes it lazy, stopping at the first place the rest of the pattern fits.

title: Anchors
text: ^ anchors a match to the start of the line and $ to the end. Without anchors a pattern matches anywhere inside the text, which is a common source of validation bugs.

title: Capture groups
text: Parentheses capture the text a subpattern matched so you can extract or reference it later. Named groups give each capture a label instead of a number.

title: Character classes
text: Square brackets match one character from a set, like [0-9a-f] for a hex digit. A leading ^ inside the brackets negates the set to mean anything except these.

title: Lookahead and lookbehind
text: Lookarounds assert that text appears before or after the current position without consuming it. They enable rules like a password must contain a digit checked in one pattern.

title: Catastrophic backtracking
text: Nested quantifiers can force a regex engine to try exponentially many paths, hanging the process on crafted input. This catastrophic backtracking is a denial of service risk; prefer simpler patterns or a timeout.

title: Escaping special characters
text: Characters like dot, plus and parentheses have meaning in a pattern and must be escaped with a backslash to match literally. Most languages ship an escape helper so user input can be embedded safely.

title: Profile before optimizing
text: Measure where time is actually spent before rewriting anything. Optimizing without a profiler usually speeds up code that was never the bottleneck while the slow path stays slow.

title: Big-O intuition
text: Complexity describes how cost grows with input size: a nested loop over the same data is quadratic and falls over as the data grows. An algorithm that is fine at a thousand items can be hopeless at a million.

title: Memoization
text: Memoization stores the result of an expensive function keyed by its arguments. A later call with arguments already seen returns the stored answer immediately.

title: Lazy loading
text: Lazy loading defers fetching a resource until it is actually needed, shortening the initial load. Images below the fold and rarely used code are the classic candidates.

title: Batching small operations
text: A thousand tiny writes or requests cost far more than one batch carrying the same data, because each round trip pays fixed overhead. Batching amortizes that overhead across the whole group.

title: Feature flags
text: A feature flag toggles behavior at runtime without a deploy, letting you ship dark code and turn it on gradually. Flags double as kill switches when a rollout goes wrong.

title: Fast CI pipelines
text: A CI pipeline should run the cheapest checks first so obvious failures surface in seconds. Caching dependencies and running suites in parallel keeps the whole run short enough that people wait for it.
